fatal_errors: The proposed annealing-versus-quenching intervention does not reconstruct the target temperature-dependent single-crystal compression, strain-rate-jump, TEM, and DFT comparison.

The short-range-order/shear-fault-energy mechanism replaces the target mechanisms of MSAD-controlled solid-solution resistance, cryogenic inertial dulling, and high-temperature Cottrell-type solute pinning.
No specific alloy compositions, crystal orientation, deformation temperatures, strain rates, or quantitative predictions are given.
Annealing can change vacancies, dislocation density, segregation, precipitation, and other microstructural variables, so the proposed comparison does not isolate short-range order.
No cited evidence supports the asserted link between annealing, short-range order, local shear-fault-energy fluctuations, and strengthening.
explanation: The response addresses the broad question of what may govern strength in concentrated alloys and offers a testable alternative centered on short-range order. Its matched-composition annealed-versus-quenched comparison and microscopy/diffraction measurements are directionally reasonable. However, it does not recover the target study's alloys, temperature range, crystallographic compression geometry, CRSS measurements, strain-rate jumps, or quantitative trends. It also misses all three central target conclusions: lattice-distortion/MSAD scaling of extrapolated strength, phonon-drag-related inertial dulling below roughly 60–77 K, and Mn/Fe-dependent Portevin–Le Chatelier strengthening at high temperature. The experiment is only moderately discriminating because heat treatment changes multiple variables and the proposed local shear-fault-energy fluctuations are measured only indirectly. The falsification criterion is qualitative and bundles several outcomes, while the supporting evidence is uncited.
